1956 Chrysler New Yorker Parked for Decades Is a Rare St. Regis, a Sad Sight
10 photos
Photo: Bobs Classic Cars & Parts/YouTube
Introduced in 1940, the Chrysler New Yorker remained in continuous production through 1996 (minus the WW2 years). It served as the brand's flagship model, and it's Chrysler's longest-running nameplate . It also spawned a few cool limited-edition vehicles, including the St. Regis.
The most recent Mopar to sport the St. Regis badge was actually a Dodge. The full-size car was offered between 1979 and 1981. However, it also graced the New Yorker on two occasions. Chrysler sold one between 1974 and 1978, while the original version hit dealerships in 1955 and 1956.
The St. Regis arrived on the fourth-generation New Yorker, which was a significant departure from its predecessor. The 1955 luxury car had its design based on the custom 1952 Imperial Parade Phaeton limo, which was penned by Virgil Exner. The styling kicked off the Forward Look era, lasting through 1961.
The St. Regis badge was reserved for two-door hardtop models with exclusive two-tone paint. The options list also included a choice of three-tone paint schemes. The bundle also included a bit of extra chrome trim, a textured vinyl headliner, cloth upholstery inserts, and a color-keyed cabin. The St. Regis did nothing for the New Yorker in the performance department.
The model was somewhat popular for a luxury vehicle in 1955. Of the 52,178 New Yorkers delivered, exactly 11,076 had St. Regis badges. That's a little over 21% of the total output. In 1956, New Yorker deliveries dropped to 41,140 examples, with the St. Regis model finding 6,686 homes (16% of the total production).
Although it's not rare by production numbers, the original New Yorker St. Regis is a pretty rare sight nowadays. And that's because most of them are rotting away in junkyards and backyards, much like the 1956 hardtop you see here.
Spotted at an estate sale, this St. Regis rolled off the assembly line in a three-tone finish . But it's no longer a pretty sight. Parked for decades and picked for parts, the Mopar is a sad sight. The car is missing its trunk lid and the passenger door, as well as much of the interior. Unfortunately, the original drivetrain was also removed.
But we can still see that it rolled off the assembly line in a three-tone finish. It was a black roof, while the rest of the body is a white-on-red combo. I bet that this St. Regis was a gorgeous sight when it was new.
Is it worth restoring? Well, not really. A rotisserie restoration could cost up to six figures nowadays, and these Mopars don't fetch nearly as much in perfect condition at public auctions. I've seen only a couple go for over $40,000, and a few others reached into $30,000 territory. As far as I know, no St. Regis fetched beyond $50,000 (though the rarest New Yorker convertibles did on a few occasions).
Does this hardtop have a future in any form, or should it be parted out and sent to the crusher ? Check it out in the video below and tell me your thoughts in the comments section.
